subject: Neurology
subtopic: Other dementias: FTD, Lewy body, vascular, CJD, HIV
vignette: A 58-year-old woman has had 2 years of progressive personality change with disinhibition and compulsive behaviors, followed by difficulty finding words. MRI shows frontal and temporal lobe atrophy, and autopsy reveals round inclusions staining for hyperphosphorylated tau.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Frontotemporal dementia, formerly called Pick disease, presents with early changes in personality and behavior (behavioral variant) or aphasia (primary progressive aphasia) and may have associated movement disorders. Imaging shows frontal and/or temporal lobe atrophy, and histology shows inclusions of hyperphosphorylated tau (round Pick bodies) or ubiquitinated TDP-43. This patient's early behavioral change and aphasia with frontotemporal atrophy and tau-positive Pick bodies are classic.

explanation_incorrect.A: Alzheimer disease typically begins with memory impairment and shows Aβ plaques and tau tangles with hippocampal atrophy, not early personality change and Pick bodies.
explanation_incorrect.B: Lewy body dementia features visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition, REM behavior disorder, and parkinsonism with cortical Lewy bodies.
explanation_incorrect.C: Vascular dementia produces stepwise decline after multiple infarcts rather than slowly progressive behavioral and language change.
explanation_incorrect.E: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is rapidly progressive over weeks to months with startle myoclonus, ataxia, and spongiform cortex.

educationalObjective: Recognize frontotemporal dementia by early behavioral or language changes, frontotemporal atrophy, and Pick bodies of hyperphosphorylated tau.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Other dementias: FTD, Lewy body, vascular, CJD, HIV
vignette: A 67-year-old man has recurrent vivid visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition and alertness from day to day, and REM sleep behavior disorder in which he acts out his dreams. He also has mild parkinsonism. Cognitive and motor symptoms began about 6 months apart, and autopsy shows intracellular Lewy bodies primarily in the cortex.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Lewy body dementia is characterized by visual hallucinations, dementia with fluctuating cognition or alertness, REM sleep behavior disorder, and parkinsonism, with intracellular Lewy bodies primarily in the cortex. It is termed Lewy body dementia when cognitive and motor symptom onset are less than 1 year apart; otherwise it is considered dementia secondary to Parkinson disease. This patient's hallucinations, fluctuations, dream enactment, parkinsonism, and 6-month interval between cognitive and motor onset fit the diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Dementia secondary to Parkinson disease is diagnosed when cognitive symptoms begin more than 1 year after motor symptoms, unlike this 6-month interval.
explanation_incorrect.C: Alzheimer disease presents with progressive memory loss and cortical Aβ plaques and tau tangles, not fluctuating hallucinations and REM behavior disorder.
explanation_incorrect.D: Frontotemporal dementia begins with personality, behavior, or language changes and frontal/temporal atrophy, not visual hallucinations and parkinsonism.
explanation_incorrect.E: Vascular dementia shows stepwise decline with multiple infarcts on imaging, not the fluctuating cognitive and hallucinatory picture described.

educationalObjective: Diagnose Lewy body dementia from visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition, REM behavior disorder, and parkinsonism with onset less than 1 year apart.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Other dementias: FTD, Lewy body, vascular, CJD, HIV
vignette: A 64-year-old man develops dementia that progresses over 6 weeks, with exaggerated startle-induced muscle jerks and gait ataxia. EEG shows periodic sharp-wave complexes, CSF testing shows elevated 14-3-3 protein, and autopsy shows spongiform cortex with vacuolation and no inflammation.
question: Which of the following best describes the cause of this disease?

options.text: Accumulation of extracellular Aβ plaques and intracellular tau tangles
Multiple arterial infarcts producing stepwise cognitive decline
Conversion of PrPc to PrPsc, a β-pleated sheet resistant to proteases
Microglial nodules with multinucleated giant cells from advanced HIV infection
Expansion of CAG repeats in the huntingtin gene

explanation_correct: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is caused by prions, in which normal PrPc is converted to PrPsc, a β-pleated sheet conformation resistant to proteases. It produces rapidly progressive dementia over weeks to months with startle myoclonus and ataxia and is fatal. It is typically sporadic but can be transmitted by contaminated materials such as corneal transplants or neurosurgical equipment. Spongiform cortex with vacuolation without inflammation, periodic sharp waves on EEG, and elevated CSF 14-3-3 protein are characteristic findings.

explanation_incorrect.A: Aβ plaques and tau tangles are features of Alzheimer disease, which progresses over years rather than weeks.
explanation_incorrect.B: Multiple arterial infarcts cause vascular dementia with stepwise decline and infarcts on imaging, not spongiform cortex and periodic EEG complexes.
explanation_incorrect.D: Microglial nodules with multinucleated giant cells are characteristic of HIV-associated dementia, not a rapidly fatal spongiform encephalopathy.
explanation_incorrect.E: CAG repeat expansion in HTT causes Huntington disease, a chronic movement disorder with chorea and caudate atrophy.

educationalObjective: Identify Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease as a fatal prion (PrPc to PrPsc) dementia with rapid course, startle myoclonus, spongiform cortex, and positive 14-3-3.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Other dementias: FTD, Lewy body, vascular, CJD, HIV
vignette: A 70-year-old man with long-standing hypertension and diabetes mellitus has had cognitive decline occurring in distinct stepwise drops, each following a small clinical stroke, with late-onset memory impairment. CT shows multiple cortical and subcortical infarcts.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Vascular dementia is the second most common cause of dementia in older adults and results from multiple arterial infarcts and/or chronic ischemia. It causes a stepwise decline in cognitive ability with late-onset memory impairment, and imaging shows multiple cortical and/or subcortical infarcts. This patient's stepwise deterioration with vascular risk factors and multiple infarcts on CT is classic. Alzheimer disease, by contrast, produces a smooth progressive decline rather than discrete stepwise drops.

explanation_incorrect.B: Alzheimer disease causes gradual, continuous decline with cortical atrophy, Aβ plaques, and tau tangles rather than stepwise neurologic deficits.
explanation_incorrect.C: Lewy body dementia features fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, REM behavior disorder, and parkinsonism, not stepwise infarcts.
explanation_incorrect.D: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease progresses over weeks to months with startle myoclonus and spongiform cortex, not over years with discrete strokes.
explanation_incorrect.E: Frontotemporal dementia begins with personality or language changes and frontotemporal atrophy rather than vascular events.

educationalObjective: Recognize vascular dementia as the second most common dementia, with stepwise decline and multiple infarcts on imaging.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Other dementias: FTD, Lewy body, vascular, CJD, HIV
vignette: A 38-year-old man with advanced HIV infection and a low CD4 count has cognitive deficits, a wide-based gait disturbance, irritability, and depressed mood. Imaging shows diffuse gray matter and subcortical atrophy, and brain biopsy would show microglial nodules containing multinucleated giant cells.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: HIV-associated dementia is a subcortical dysfunction associated with advanced HIV infection, characterized by cognitive deficits, gait disturbance, irritability, and depressed mood. It shows diffuse gray matter and subcortical atrophy with microglial nodules containing multinucleated giant cells. This patient's advanced HIV, subcortical symptoms, and histology are characteristic. The subcortical pattern distinguishes it from the cortical dementias such as Alzheimer disease.

explanation_incorrect.A: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is a rapidly progressive fatal dementia with spongiform cortex, periodic EEG complexes, and startle myoclonus, not microglial nodules.
explanation_incorrect.B: Frontotemporal dementia features early personality and behavior changes or aphasia with frontal or temporal atrophy and Pick bodies.
explanation_incorrect.C: Alzheimer disease shows cortical atrophy with Aβ plaques and tau tangles rather than subcortical atrophy and giant-cell-rich microglial nodules.
explanation_incorrect.D: Lewy body dementia includes visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition, REM behavior disorder, and cortical Lewy bodies.

educationalObjective: Identify HIV-associated dementia as a subcortical dementia of advanced HIV with microglial nodules and multinucleated giant cells.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Other dementias: FTD, Lewy body, vascular, CJD, HIV
vignette: A 66-year-old man has had 1 year of progressive cognitive decline, a magnetic shuffling gait with difficulty initiating steps, and new urinary incontinence. Imaging shows enlarged ventricles with normal cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure and no cortical atrophy.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this reversible cause of dementia?

options.text: Depression (pseudodementia) presenting with poor effort and depressed mood
Vitamin B12 deficiency causing a megaloblastic anemia and cognitive change
Hypothyroidism with cognitive slowing and raised TSH
Normal pressure hydrocephalus with ventriculomegaly, gait apraxia, incontinence, and dementia
Neurosyphilis with a positive CSF VDRL and neurologic findings

explanation_correct: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is one of the reversible causes of dementia, which also include depression (pseudodementia), hypothyroidism, vitamin B12 deficiency, and neurosyphilis. It classically produces a triad of gait apraxia, urinary incontinence, and dementia with ventriculomegaly and normal CSF pressure, as in this patient. The combination of gait difficulty and incontinence with enlarged ventricles distinguishes it from the cortical dementias and from the other reversible causes listed.

explanation_incorrect.A: Depression (pseudodementia) causes poor effort and mood symptoms but not gait apraxia, incontinence, or ventriculomegaly.
explanation_incorrect.B: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes cognitive change with megaloblastic anemia and neurologic findings, not ventricular enlargement with normal pressure.
explanation_incorrect.C: Hypothyroidism causes reversible cognitive slowing with elevated TSH, not the gait and incontinence triad with ventriculomegaly.
explanation_incorrect.E: Neurosyphilis is a reversible cause of dementia with a positive CSF VDRL, but it does not produce the classic ventriculomegaly and gait apraxia described.

educationalObjective: Identify normal pressure hydrocephalus as a reversible dementia with the triad of gait apraxia, urinary incontinence, and ventriculomegaly at normal pressure.
